newsitem.title: UK: Sterling spirals ever lower in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Sterling spirals ever lower in late Europe.

text.p: Sterling was looking more than a little battered at the end of its first full week under a Labour government after an alleged mugging by a member of the new administration.

It perked up on the radical move to Bank of England independence after Labour swept to power on May 1, but comments by an unnamed Labour source saying sterling should re-enter the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) at 2.50 marks sent it reeling in the latter part of this week.
From Tuesday's peak the pound has come down nearly seven pfennigs to 2.76 and two cents to $1.62, with its trade weighted index down 1.5 points at 99.1.
This is no bad thing for Britain's exporters, who are already beginning to feel the pinch of higher sterling on their competitiveness abroad.

While the government would certainly be happy to see sterling lower, particularly against the European currencies, it was only an alleged mugging because a mugging is a deliberate act and implies malice aforethought.
There is certainly a theory in the market that the comment was aimed at taking some of the steam out of sterling, but most believe it was probably down to loose-tongued inexperience.
The new Treasury team were certainly keen to distance themselves from the remark saying "There is no truth in it at all."
But, as analysts said, they would say that, wouldn't they.
"This is certainly not the way to indulge in verbal intervention," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
"It does smack of naivety and whoever said it has probably got his or her knuckles rapped because it simply injected volatility, and that's the last thing the government wants."
Analysts said even if it was an off-the-cuff remark and Labour sources do not keep popping up talking about lower levels, the fundamental background is anyway starting to point to an easier pound.

In another quick move by the new government, interest rates were raised a quarter point to 6.25 percent and although independence for the Bank of England might on the face of it point to a more cautionary monetary stance, there is a growing feeling that fiscal policy will soon be taking the strain.
"U.K. rates are still probably going to go up but perhaps not as high as previously thought," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered.
He noted that there was a growing perception that rates elsewhere in the world were going up and particularly about the next move in Japan.
"In the past environment sterling has been a major beneficiary of other countries low level of interest rates but perceptions are starting to change" he said.
"Beneath everything else that has been swirling around this week, the perceptions about not only U.K. rates but also rates elsewhere are starting to change."

Labour are perceived as being more pro-Europe than the old Conservative administration, and while ERM membership is a prerequisite for joining a single currency, analysts very much doubt that sterling will re-enter at an early stage.
"We think talk about near-term ERM entry is completely unrealistic," said Tony Norfield, Treasury Economist at ABN-Amro.
"The new government has said that 1999 EMU participation is unlikely so there is no reason to consider ERM membership for at least one or two years," he added.
Also, talking sterling down goes against the grain given that the newly independent Bank of England has a remit to keep inflation down.
Artificially managing the currency down would clearly be inconsistent with this target, analysts said.
"And it's a very dangerous game," warned Ian Amstad, International Economist at Bankers Trust.
"When you start talking your currency down it can lead to an accident."
